header: MANS-HIS-203 · Physiology — leukocyte/innate-immunity function, authored from the His Continuous Berlin Book 2026's "Physio HIS 2" past-exam block (p.112-115), printed keys. Four questions test three new mints (neutrophil first-line/myeloperoxidase/diapedesis bundled, agranulocytosis/leukaemia, tissue-macrophage nomenclature/ameboid movement, granulocyte/monocyte lifespan); two reuse existing live concepts (chemotaxis, opsonins).

questions.title: First line of defense against bacterial infection
questions.question: What is the first line of defense against bacterial infections?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Basophils mediate immediate (type I) hypersensitivity through IgE-triggered histamine release; they are not the first phagocytic responder to bacterial infection.
explanations.B: Correct. Neutrophils are the most numerous circulating granulocyte and the first phagocytic cell to arrive at a bacterial infection site, making them the innate immune system's first line of defence. They are recruited rapidly by chemotaxis, cross the capillary wall by diapedesis, and kill the ingested bacterium using myeloperoxidase and other granule contents once phagocytosed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eosinophils are specialised against large parasites (helminths) and participate in allergic reactions; bacterial defence is not their primary role.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Monocytes (and the tissue macrophages they become) are important phagocytes but arrive later than neutrophils and are not considered the first line of defence.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lymphocytes mediate adaptive, antigen-specific immunity, which takes days to develop; they play no role in the immediate innate response to bacteria.

questions.subtopic: Innate immunity — phagocyte recruitment and killing
questions.learning_objective: Identify neutrophils as the first-line phagocytic defence against bacterial infection.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.112

questions.title: Enzyme that kills ingested bacteria in neutrophils
questions.question: Which enzyme is present in neutrophils and kills the ingested bacteria?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase speeds the interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate in erythrocytes; it plays no part in neutrophil bacterial killing.
explanations.B: Correct. Myeloperoxidase, carried in the neutrophil's azurophilic granules, combines with hydrogen peroxide and a halide (chloride) to generate hypochlorous acid and other potent oxidants once a bacterium has been phagocytosed into a phagosome. This oxidative killing mechanism is central to the neutrophil's ability to destroy ingested organisms, and its absence (myeloperoxidase deficiency) predisposes to certain fungal infections.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histaminase degrades histamine and is associated with eosinophils, not with intracellular bacterial killing in neutrophils.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase supports the NADPH-generating pentose phosphate pathway that feeds the oxidative burst, but it is not itself the enzyme that directly kills the ingested bacterium.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Major basic protein is an eosinophil granule constituent toxic mainly to parasites, not a neutrophil bacterial-killing enzyme.

questions.subtopic: Innate immunity — phagocyte recruitment and killing
questions.learning_objective: Identify myeloperoxidase as the neutrophil enzyme responsible for killing ingested bacteria.

questions.title: WBC movement through the capillary wall into tissue
questions.question: Which step in phagocytosis involves the movement of white blood cells through the capillary wall into tissue spaces?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phagosome formation is the step in which the ingested particle is enclosed within a membrane-bound vesicle inside the phagocyte, occurring after the cell has already reached the target, not the vessel-crossing step itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chemotaxis is directed movement along a chemical gradient toward the infection site; it describes the direction of travel, not the specific act of crossing the capillary wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen with molecules (antibody, complement) that facilitate its recognition and uptake by phagocytes, unrelated to crossing the vessel wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Margination is the preceding step in which the leukocyte rolls along and adheres to the vessel wall, positioning it for the crossing that follows — it precedes diapedesis rather than being the crossing itself.
explanations.E: Correct. Diapedesis is the specific step in which the neutrophil physically squeezes between adjacent endothelial cells of the capillary wall, moving from the bloodstream into the tissue space. It occurs immediately after margination (rolling and adhesion against the vessel wall) and before the cell reaches the infection site by chemotaxis. This three-step sequence — margination, diapedesis, chemotaxis — is how a circulating neutrophil gets from blood to a tissue infection site.

questions.subtopic: Innate immunity — phagocyte recruitment and killing
questions.learning_objective: Identify diapedesis as the step in which a leukocyte crosses the capillary wall into tissue, as distinct from margination, chemotaxis and opsonization.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.113

questions.title: Movement of phagocytic cells in response to a chemical stimulus
questions.question: Movement of phagocytic cells in response to chemical stimulus is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Chemotaxis is the directed movement of a phagocyte along a rising chemical gradient — bacterial products, complement fragments, or cytokines — toward the site generating that signal. It is the mechanism that brings a neutrophil or macrophage from the circulation to an infection site once it has crossed into tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen with molecules that facilitate its recognition and uptake by phagocytes, a separate step from the movement itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ingestion is the phagocyte's engulfment of the target once it has already reached it, not the directed movement toward it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Digestion is the intracellular breakdown of the ingested material after phagocytosis, occurring well after the movement described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tolerance describes the immune system's non-response to self or harmless antigens, an unrelated adaptive-immunity concept.

questions.learning_objective: Define chemotaxis as directed phagocyte movement toward a chemical stimulus.

questions.title: Marrow failure to produce WBCs
questions.question: Name of condition through which bone marrow fails to produce WBCs leaving body unprotected against infection is

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaemia is a reduction in red cell mass or haemoglobin, unrelated to white cell production or infection risk.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Leucopenia is the general term for any low white cell count, from many possible causes; it lacks the specific marrow-production-failure mechanism and severe infection-risk implication this condition names.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Leukocytosis is a raised, not lowered, white cell count — the opposite direction from what this question describes.
explanations.D: Correct. Agranulocytosis is bone-marrow failure to produce granulocytes (mainly neutrophils), a severe and clinically dangerous condition that leaves the body essentially unprotected against bacterial and fungal infection. It is distinguished from ordinary leucopenia by both its severity and its specific marrow-production mechanism, and is a recognised drug-induced medical emergency (for example with certain antithyroid or antipsychotic drugs).
explanations.E: Incorrect. Polycythemia is an increased, not decreased, red cell count and is unrelated to white cell production.

questions.learning_objective: Identify agranulocytosis as bone-marrow failure to produce granulocytes, leaving the body unprotected against infection.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.113

questions.title: Uncontrolled production of WBCs
questions.question: Uncontrolled production of WBCs (very high number) is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leukocytosis is an ordinary, reactive rise in white cell count (as in infection), without malignant transformation — a milder, physiological process compared to what this question describes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymphocytosis names a raised lymphocyte count specifically, a narrower and usually reactive finding, not the uncontrolled malignant proliferation described here.
explanations.C: Correct. Leukaemia is the uncontrolled, malignant proliferation of white blood cells or their marrow precursors, producing a very high circulating white cell count. This is distinct from leukocytosis, which is an ordinary reactive rise without malignant transformation, and from lymphocytosis, a narrower reactive rise limited to lymphocytes. The malignant clone in leukaemia also displaces normal marrow elements, which is why leukaemia typically presents with anaemia and thrombocytopenia alongside the abnormal white cell count.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leukopenia is a low, not high, white cell count — the opposite direction from what this question describes.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish leukaemia (malignant, uncontrolled WBC proliferation) from ordinary leukocytosis.

questions.title: Example of a tissue macrophage
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a tissue macrophage?

options.B: Red blood cells in the bloodstream

explanations.A: Correct. Kupffer cells are the resident, monocyte-derived tissue macrophage population lining the hepatic sinusoids of the liver. They phagocytose bacteria, debris and aged blood cells arriving from the portal circulation, giving the liver an important role in systemic immune surveillance. Kupffer cells are one of several organ-specific tissue-macrophage names this bank tests, alongside microglia in the CNS, alveolar macrophages in the lung, and osteoclasts in bone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Red blood cells are anucleate, non-phagocytic cells whose function is oxygen transport, not a macrophage population.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Platelets are cell fragments from megakaryocytes involved in haemostasis, not a phagocytic tissue macrophage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteocytes are the mature, non-phagocytic bone-maintaining cell derived from osteoblasts; the bone's own tissue-macrophage-lineage cell is instead the osteoclast.

questions.learning_objective: Name Kupffer cells as the liver's tissue-macrophage population.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.114

questions.title: Tissue macrophage of the central nervous system
questions.question: Which type of tissue macrophage is found in the central nervous system?

explanations.A: Correct. Microglia are the resident, macrophage-lineage phagocyte of the central nervous system. They continuously survey neural tissue at rest and become activated to phagocytose debris and pathogens when injury or infection occurs. Microglia are distinct from the CNS's other glial cell types (astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells), none of which are phagocytic in the same primary sense.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Alveolar macrophages are the lung airspace's resident macrophage population, not the CNS's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Kupffer cells are the liver's resident macrophage population, not the CNS's.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Langerhans cells are the skin epidermis's dendritic-cell population, not the CNS's tissue macrophage.

questions.learning_objective: Name microglia as the CNS's tissue-macrophage population.

questions.title: Locomotion mechanism of tissue macrophages and fibroblasts at a wound
questions.question: Asim, a 5 years old boy falls from his bicycle and receives a cut over the knee. His tissue macrophages & fibroblasts will move to the site of injury for repair by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ciliary movement is the coordinated beating of cilia (as on respiratory epithelium) that moves fluid or mucus over a stationary cell surface, not the locomotion of an individual migrating cell.
explanations.B: Correct. Tissue macrophages and fibroblasts converging on a wound migrate by ameboid movement — the same flowing, pseudopod-driven locomotion an amoeba uses. The cell extends and retracts cytoplasmic projections (pseudopods) to crawl through tissue toward the site of injury, rather than using cilia or a flagellum. This is the general locomotion mechanism for connective-tissue and immune cells migrating through tissue, not a specialised mechanism unique to any one cell type.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chemotaxis names the directional cue (moving along a chemical gradient) rather than the physical locomotion mechanism itself, which is ameboid movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Margination is the vascular step in which a leukocyte adheres to the endothelium before crossing into tissue; it does not describe locomotion through tissue toward a wound.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Whip-like (flagellar) movement propels cells such as spermatozoa or certain protozoa, not migrating macrophages or fibroblasts.

questions.learning_objective: Identify ameboid movement as the locomotion mechanism tissue macrophages and fibroblasts use to migrate to a site of injury.

questions.title: Definition of opsonins
questions.question: Opsonins are molecules that:

options.A: Are secreted by neutrophils to kill pathogens
options.B: Attach to pathogens to facilitate their recognition and uptake by neutrophils
options.C: Block the phagocytic receptors on neutrophils
options.D: Inhibit the release of inflammatory mediators by neutrophils

explanations.A: Incorrect. Opsonins coat the pathogen itself rather than being secreted killing agents; the neutrophil's own granule enzymes (such as myeloperoxidase) are what actually kill the ingested organism.
explanations.B: Correct. Opsonins (such as antibody or complement fragments like C3b) attach to a pathogen's surface, coating it in a way that phagocyte surface receptors specifically recognise. This coating markedly increases the efficiency of recognition and uptake compared with unopsonised phagocytosis — a process called opsonization. Opsonization is a key link between the adaptive immune system (antibody) or complement cascade and the effector phagocytosis carried out by neutrophils and macrophages.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Opsonins promote, rather than block, phagocytic receptor engagement — this option describes the opposite of their function.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Opsonins act on recognition and uptake, not on suppressing inflammatory mediator release.

questions.learning_objective: Define opsonins as molecules that coat pathogens to facilitate their recognition and uptake by phagocytes.

questions.title: Average life span of granulocytes
questions.question: The average life span for granulocytes is:

explanations.A: Correct. Granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) have a short average circulating life span of about 4-5 days from release into the blood to their eventual destruction or migration into tissue. This short lifespan reflects their role as rapidly deployed, short-lived first-responder cells, in contrast to the erythrocyte's much longer 120-day lifespan. Continuous marrow production is therefore needed to sustain a normal granulocyte count, which is why marrow suppression causes granulocyte counts to fall within days.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 12-14 days is longer than the granulocyte's actual short circulating life span.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 4-5 weeks is far longer than the granulocyte's actual life span and is not a standard reference value for any major blood cell.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 120 days is the erythrocyte's life span, not the granulocyte's — a common distractor pairing in this bank's numeric reference-range questions.

questions.learning_objective: State that the granulocyte's average circulating life span is about 4-5 days.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.113

questions.title: Leukocyte with the longest life span
questions.question: Which of the following WBCs have the longest life span?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Neutrophils, despite being the most numerous leukocyte, circulate for only about 4-5 days on average — one of the shortest leukocyte lifespans, not the longest.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Eosinophils circulate briefly, similar to other granulocytes, and do not have the longest leukocyte life span.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Basophils, like other granulocytes, are short-lived in circulation and do not have the longest leukocyte life span.
explanations.D: Correct. Monocytes have the longest circulating life span among the leukocytes, spending a comparatively long period in the blood before migrating into tissue. Once in tissue they differentiate into the long-lived tissue macrophage population (such as Kupffer cells or microglia), extending their functional lifespan far beyond that of the short-lived granulocytes. This contrast — numerous but short-lived granulocytes versus less numerous but long-lived monocytes — is the distinction this bank tests.

questions.learning_objective: Identify monocytes as the leukocyte with the longest circulating life span.
